channel — the pushed value

The third primitive, and the one most people meet only through its transport. Where state is owned and memo is pulled, a channel is pushed: publish(message) appends to a topic and iterating it subscribes. It ships from abide/shared/channel, so it is isomorphic like the other two — a browser module can own a channel and fan messages out locally exactly as a server module can, and both are on this page. Nothing here opens a connection: the point of this page is the primitive before any transport.

Two operations, and you have seen the primitive: publish a message, iterate to receive it. The {'{'}#for await{'}'} block is the subscription — no connection to open, no handler to register.

This channel's room type is void, so the message is publish's only argument. Declare a room and it comes back in front of the message — the ladder below walks that rule.

A Channel<T> is an AsyncIterable<T>, so for await (const m of chatter) is the whole API — in an RPC handler, in onStart, at module scope, in a script under abide run. Iterate to subscribe; leave the loop to unsubscribe. The template block is only markup's spelling of it.

This card is the proof: nothing on the client iterates anything. The subscription is a for await in a plain server module, and the buttons only publish and read back what that loop kept. Publish "stop" and the loop breaks — publishing after that reaches no one.

Iterated inside an SSR page render, a channel yields its tail snapshot and then completes — a live topic has no end, so a render that waited for one would never finish. Everywhere else on the server the same loop stays open until you break out of it.

A non-void Args gives per-room topics — channel({'{'}room{'}'}) subscribes one, publish({'{'}room{'}'}, msg) addresses one — each a distinct hub created lazily. It is the mechanism a memo uses to keep one slot per args: rooms are the primitive's key, not a socket feature bolted on. Publish into a room you are not watching and nothing shows up.

This card is owned by a browser module, so its rooms never leave the page. A server module keys its rooms identically; a socket is what carries one of those to a browser, and it changes none of this.

The cards above both call publish and do not agree on its arity — that is the point. The key is a positional that exists only when the callable declared an input, so the call shrinks as you climb down this ladder. publish is declared once on the shared surface, so a memo and a socket obey the same rule — socket.publish(msg) was never the transport doing you a favour.

The other verbs got this free — a void parameter is omittable, so peek() / chunks() / invalidate() collapsed on their own. publish and watch carry a trailing payload, which is the only place the key had to be made to vanish deliberately.

One .abide caveat, unrelated to the rule: an argless memo bound in a template auto-calls, so d is its value and the memo's own surface is not reachable through that binding — which is why the middle rung uses a keyed memo. In plain .ts, publish(value) on an argless memo is exactly what you write.

tail is the one retention knob — how many recent messages a late joiner replays before going live. The card above keeps nothing; this one sets tail: 3, which is also what makes its chunks() probe non-empty.

A channel implements the identical vocabulary a memo does — peek / chunks / pending / refreshing / error / done, plus refresh / invalidate / publish / watch. That is the argument of ADR 0023: two honest storage strategies behind one surface, so a caller never branches on which it holds. Here peek() is the latest message and chunks() the tail transcript.

On this in-process core the status probes are degenerate — a local topic is immediately live, never reconnecting and never errored — and peek/chunks read the hub directly, so this card snapshots them on a button. Putting the channel on the wire is what makes them reactive: see socket probes.

Everything here is local. socket = channel + transport + per-room authorization; the pub/sub core, the rooms and the read surface are all this primitive, unchanged. Continue at sockets.

Global probes

The per-slot probes read one memo. These are their app-wide siblings — probes and verbs that act across slots or over the whole process: reachable(host) and online() report connectivity, and the tag selectors (invalidate({'{'}tags{'}'}) / refresh({'{'}tags{'}'})) drop or revalidate every slot carrying a tag at once.

reachable(host) actively probes a host: the app's own origin answers (true), a dead local port is refused (false).

online() is a reactive connectivity boolean — always true on the server, tracks navigator.onLine in the browser. No args, no slot: app-wide state read straight in a template.

Two shared reads carry the tag "docs". The global verb invalidate({'{'} tags: ["docs"] {'}'}) — run server-side through a POST RPC, so the drop is observable in one pass — drops both slots at once, so a re-read of each re-fetches together.

The eager sibling: refresh({'{'} tags: ["docs"] {'}'}) revalidates every tagged slot in place, retaining each stale value while it re-runs — so a re-read returns a freshly climbed count.

The read side of the tag surface: reactive aggregates that are true if any slot carrying a tag is loading or revalidating. Like the tag verbs, they're isomorphic — tags no longer require crossRequest, so a tagged read registers its browser memo too and these answer on either side. This demo reaches them over an RPC only because a server pass can observe the whole transition deterministically, in one go: a tagged read goes pending while it first loads, then refreshing while it revalidates over the retained value.
src/ui/pages/memo/page.abide:
memo — the loaded value

The second primitive: one memoizer covering everything derived. A memo's dependencies are its declared inputs (ADR 0024) — declare args and they are the cache key; declare none and they are inferred from what the body reads. That single rule spans a synchronous derivation off a state and an async slot with cache, coalescing, and a reactive read surface. It is why there is no separate computed or linked primitive, and why rpc = memo + transport.

An argless, synchronous body is auto-tracked: it subscribes to whatever it reads and recomputes lazily. Its bare call returns T, not a promise, so it renders in the initial HTML instead of blanking and refilling a microtask later. Drive count and doubled follows, updating only its text node.

Pass a thunk and what it reads becomes the whole dependency set: memo(source, transform) tracks the thunk only, and the transform runs untracked — so a transform can read anything without that read becoming a trigger. Here it reads factor, so bumping factor alone recomputes nothing; the next change to count picks up its current value.

The source is always a thunk (ADR 0025), which is why there is no dependency-declaring syntax to learn: the tracked region is an arrow body you can point at. Same rule as watch(source, handler).

Several inputs need no API of their own — they are what the thunk returns. Every read inside it is tracked, and the transform still receives ONE argument. Return an object and they stay named, so adding an input never shifts the others.

A memo derives, it doesn't hold — .state() projects one back into a writable cell whose set IS publish, so a local write is provisional and holds only until the next re-fill. That is the shape behind every editable field seeded from loaded data: the draft seeds to count × 100, bumping it edits locally, and changing count reseeds and discards those edits.

Declare an argument and it becomes the cache key, so the memo keeps one slot per key — {'{'} w: 3, h: 4 {'}'} and {'{'} w: 2, h: 5 {'}'} are independent, each reused on the next read with the same key.

The args are then the whole dependency set, so the body runs untracked. A synchronous body stays synchronous: the read is the value, not a promise, so it renders straight into the server HTML.

The other axis — an async body. No args again, so it is one slot, but a loaded one: the read is coalesced (concurrent callers share one run), the settled value is retained, and the slot carries the full read surface (peek/pending/refreshing/error/watch + refresh/invalidate/publish).

What that costs: an argless async body is NOT auto-tracked. Half-tracked is worse than untracked, so a load re-fills on refresh/invalidate only. Read again and the run count holds, rename and nothing re-runs, refresh re-runs and picks up the current label.

Both axes at once, and nothing new to learn: the async body of the card above, keyed like the card before it. One loaded slot becomes one loaded slot per key — alpha and beta load independently, and invalidate({'{'} key: "alpha" {'}'}) drops that slot alone. This is exactly the shape an RPC takes: rpc = memo + transport, and the transport is the only difference.

state and memo live in abide/shared/*, so neither is client-only. A server module can own a state while other modules import it, derive from it (memo) and subscribe to it (watch) — a reactive graph running entirely on the server. Here two RPCs write and read one cell in $shared/serverReactive.

The server tab spells out total() and total.set(x): there is no compiler in a plain .ts, so you call the State surface directly. Same cell either way — the bare-identifier form is .abide sugar.

Module-level server state is process-global (one value across all requests) — right for a global like this counter; for mutable per-request or per-user state reach for memo: {'{'} shared {'}'}, which is guarded and identity-safe.

Reactive probes

Every memo exposes the same reactive read surface — the probes. They are views of one slot's state machine (idle → pending → value | error, with a refreshing flag over a retained value). A channel implements the same surface over a lossy hub, so this identical vocabulary shows up on RPC reads (memo + transport) and sockets (channel + transport) too — here each probe runs over a plain client-side memo(), one demo apiece.

undefined while the first load is in flight, the value once it resolves. Reading it subscribes the caller and kicks a coalesced load.

yes only while the first load runs (no value yet); back to no once the slot settles.

Distinct from pending: yes only while a re-fetch runs over a value that stays on screen. Load, then refresh — the value holds, refreshing flips to yes, pending stays no.

A rejected load lands on the slot; error() holds it until an invalidate + successful read clears it.

Runs the callback whenever this slot's value changes (unlike watch(thunk), which auto-tracks an expression). Every load and refresh fires it.
src/ui/pages/memo/verbs/page.abide:
Surface verbs

The verbs are shared by every memo and every channel — and therefore by the two transports built on them, rpc and sockets. A read is just a memo slot: reuse it, refresh it over the stale value, invalidate it to force a lazy re-fetch, publish it in place. This page is the verbs and the retention behaviour (partial match, shared, ttl); the reactive probes and the global tag selectors have their own pages. Every demo below drives a real RPC (in-process on the server, a fetch from the browser).

Before any verb, the behaviour they act on. The server counts how many times the handler actually ran. Read again and again — the count holds because the slot is reused. invalidate drops the slot, so the next read re-fetches and the count climbs.

The opposite of the default: memo: false opts a call OUT of the memo entirely — every call runs, on both sides (no retain, no coalesced reuse, no client cache). Read both here: the memo: false counter climbs on every read while the default cached one holds. (A memo: false mutation is the same — every call runs, at-least-once; a FormData body always bypasses too, since it can't be cache-keyed.)

Now the two that act on one slot's value. invalidate drops it — the lazy one, re-fetching on the next read. Slots are keyed by the whole args object. Load all three slots, then invalidate the partial selector {'{'} team: "red" {'}'} — it matches every superset slot, so both red slots re-fetch (their run counts climb together) while blue is untouched.

publish is the other direction: instead of dropping the value, write it. Load once (the server run count is small), then publish the slot value in place. Value-form sets it to 999; updater-form derives the next value from the current — both are local, so the handler never re-runs and no fetch happens.

The verbs act on a slot; these two decide how long a slot lives and who sees it. A shared read's slot is process-global. Each raw() is a separate request: the shared read returns the same run count both times (one handler run served both), while a per-request (non-shared) read re-runs and climbs. The shared handler is identity-independent and fail-closed.

And ttl bounds it in time. A shared read with a 700ms TTL. Two reads inside the window return the same count (served from cache); after the window elapses the next read re-runs the handler and the count climbs.

Where ttl bounds how long a value is served, the clock bounds how fast triggers may fire loads. It rate-limits explicit revalidation of a slot that already holds a value — refresh(), a tag refresh, a broadcast refresh — and the two names are two edges of ONE clock, so setting both is a construction-time error. Each burst here fires five refresh() calls inside one 400ms window: throttle fires on the leading edge and collapses the rest into one trailing load (two runs), debounce waits for quiet with every trigger restarting the window (one run). Both end up serving the same fresh value, which is exactly why this demo counts handler RUNS — a test over values cannot tell the two apart, or tell either from no clock at all.

It is per SLOT, and it does not gate a cold load (there is nothing stale to serve), an invalidate (which instead cancels a scheduled revalidation — deferring a discard would serve known-wrong data), or a ttl re-fill. During the window the retained value keeps being served, so await fn() never blocks on the deferred load and refreshing() is true. The clock is bilateral: the registry ships it to the browser proxy, so the burst above is driving the CLIENT memo's clock.

This is not how you rate-limit a read whose ARGS keep moving. The clock is per slot, so getQuery({'{'} q {'}'}) with a changing q is a cold load every time and throttle does nothing — debounce the INPUT and key the read on it: getQuery({'{'} q: slow() {'}'}).

refresh is the eager sibling of invalidate — it re-runs while keeping the stale value visible, which is what makes a refreshing flag meaningful. It is easiest to see next to the probe that reports it, so it lives on Reactive probes. Acting on many slots at once is Global probes.

A page and a layout take no props — there is no loader convention and no data argument. Everything a page needs comes from two isomorphic sources: route() for the URL and its params, and awaited reads for server data. props<T>() belongs to components, not pages.

route() is the same reactive accessor on both sides: route().params holds captured [name] segments, plus .url, .name, .kind, and .navigating. Reading a field re-renders on navigation.

Pages are files under src/ui/pages/. There is no route table and no router config — the folder chain is the URL. A page.abide is a route; a layout.abide wraps its folder and everything below it; a [name] segment captures into route().params.name. This very page is pages/pages/structure/page.abide, served at /pages/structure.

src/ui/pages/
    layout.abide          → wraps every page (the root layout)
    page.abide            → /
    about/page.abide      → /about
    users/
      layout.abide        → wraps /users and everything under it
      page.abide          → /users
      [id]/page.abide     → /users/:id   (route().params.id)
      new/page.abide      → /users/new   (exact wins over [id])

Each page.abide's route is its directory path with the filename dropped. A [name] folder is a dynamic segment; an exact route always wins over a param route at the same depth.

page.abide
A route. The URL is its folder chain.
layout.abide
Wraps its folder subtree; nests outer→inner and renders the page at its <slot/>. See Layouts.
[name]/
A dynamic segment, captured into route().params.name. See Routing.

Four filenames, and that is the whole convention. Everything else about a route — its params, its layout chain, its data — follows from where the file sits.

The same scoping rules apply in a page as in any component: a bare <script> runs per instance, <script module> runs once per module (imports, shared constants), and a <script> nested inside a block is branch-local. A <style> is component-scoped; a nested one is subtree-scoped.

A page has no props — route data arrives through the isomorphic reactive route() accessor (params, url, name, kind). See Data & props for the full data story.

  import Panel from "$ui/components/Panel.abide"
  import benchFrontend from "$server/rpc/benchFrontend"
  import benchFrontendClient from "$server/rpc/benchFrontendClient"
  import { state } from "abide/shared/state"
  import { benchBudget } from "@abide/bench/benchBudget"

  // Format a nanosecond mean into the tightest readable unit — mirrors the CLI bench's `fmtNs`.
  function fmtNs(ns) {
    if (ns >= 1e6) return (ns / 1e6).toFixed(2) + " ms"
    if (ns >= 1e3) return (ns / 1e3).toFixed(2) + " µs"
    return ns.toFixed(0) + " ns"
  }

  // abide ÷ vanilla — what the framework costs over the same DOM work written by hand. A `†` marks a row
  // whose ratio is squashed toward 1.00× by the timing loop's own floor (the render bench sets the flag).
  function fmtRatio(row) {
    if (row.ratio === null || row.ratio === undefined) return "—"
    return row.ratio.toFixed(2) + "×" + (row.nearFloor ? " †" : "")
  }

  // A bare multiplier, for the two DERIVED tables below: their ratios are computed here from figures this
  // page measured, rather than carried on a bench row that also knows whether it sat near the floor.
  function fmtX(value) {
    if (value === null || value === undefined) return "—"
    return value.toFixed(2) + "×"
  }

  function range(n) {
    const out = []
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) out.push(i)
    return out
  }

  // Per-scenario scope builders, keyed by name (lockstep with the server corpus in
  // `benchFrontendClient.ts`). A fresh object every call so no state leaks across timed ops. Interactive
  // scenarios inject `{ state, watch }` (their `<script>` reads them from scope) plus any list `seed`.
  // Their `state`/`watch` come from the BUNDLE (`mod.state`/`mod.watch`, threaded in per run) — the
  // page's own copies are a different module instance whose state the bundled effects can not track.
  // The corpus's render/mount scopes, rebuilt CLIENT-SIDE. They cannot ride the RPC payload with the
  // rest of a scenario, because a scope holds live things JSON has no form for — the `state`/`watch`
  // functions the interactive templates close over, and the `await-block` promise. So this list is
  // hand-kept in lockstep with `@abide/bench/scenarios`; adding a scenario there means adding it here.
  // The run loop throws on a name it cannot resolve rather than skipping it, so drift fails loudly.
  function scopesFor(mod) {
    return [
      { name: "static-text", scope: () => ({}) },
      { name: "interpolation", scope: () => ({ name: "Bob", count: 7 }) },
      { name: "attributes", scope: () => ({ id: "n1", href: "/x", title: "go", cls: "btn primary" }) },
      { name: "if-else", scope: () => ({ show: true, msg: "visible" }) },
      { name: "switch", scope: () => ({ color: "blue" }) },
      { name: "await-block", scope: () => ({ p: Promise.resolve("ready") }) },
      { name: "for-list-100", scope: () => ({ items: range(100) }) },
      { name: "for-list-1000", scope: () => ({ items: range(1000) }) },
      { name: "for-list-10000", scope: () => ({ items: range(10000) }) },
      { name: "nested-for-if-50", scope: () => ({ rows: range(50).map((i) => ({ id: i, on: i % 2 === 0 })) }) },
      { name: "class-style-directives", scope: () => ({ active: true, big: false, hue: "red", width: "40px" }) },
      { name: "many-interpolations", scope: () => ({ a: 1, b: 2, c: 3, d: 4, e: 5, f: 6, g: 7, h: 8 }) },
      { name: "deep-tree-10", scope: () => ({ v: "leaf" }) },
      { name: "component-list-100", scope: () => ({ items: range(100) }) },
      { name: "component-if", scope: () => ({ show: true, msg: "visible" }) },
      { name: "state-update", scope: () => ({ state: mod.state, watch: mod.watch }) },
      { name: "list-append-update", scope: () => ({ state: mod.state, watch: mod.watch }) },
      { name: "list-reverse-1000", scope: () => ({ state: mod.state, watch: mod.watch }) },
      { name: "if-toggle", scope: () => ({ state: mod.state, watch: mod.watch }) },
      { name: "component-if-toggle", scope: () => ({ state: mod.state, watch: mod.watch }) },
      { name: "list-swap-1000", scope: () => ({ state: mod.state, watch: mod.watch }) },
      { name: "component-list-swap-1000", scope: () => ({ state: mod.state, watch: mod.watch }) },
      { name: "list-remove-1000", scope: () => ({ state: mod.state, watch: mod.watch }) },
      { name: "list-partial-update-1000", scope: () => ({ state: mod.state, watch: mod.watch }) },
      { name: "list-select-1000", scope: () => ({ state: mod.state, watch: mod.watch }) },
      { name: "list-replace-1000", scope: () => ({ state: mod.state, watch: mod.watch }) },
      { name: "list-clear-1000", scope: () => ({ state: mod.state, watch: mod.watch }) },
    ]
  }

  // The SAME stop rule the CLI runners use — imported, not mirrored. One copy of the policy, two
  // surfaces, so their numbers stay comparable.
  //
  // A shorter budget than the CLI's, because this one runs on page load. `maxWallMs` is what keeps that
  // promise: every loop below times only PART of its round (each rebuilds a host outside the clock), and
  // when the timed half is the cheap one the two diverge hard — `unmount` times a teardown costing a
  // fifth of the mount it must do first, so a pure sample floor spent ~550ms of untimed mounting per
  // scenario per side. The extra samples buy nothing a few hundred repetitions have not already bought.
  const BUDGET = { minTimeMs: 100, minIters: 10, maxWallMs: 100 }
  const WARMUP = 3
  const UPDATES_PER_ROUND = 20

  // Let the reactive scheduler's queued microtask land the DOM patch before the next timed op.
  function flush() {
    return Promise.resolve().then(() => Promise.resolve())
  }

  // Adaptive mount timing (browser). A fresh DETACHED host per op, so no state accumulates and no
  // layout/paint is triggered (the host is never in the document). Only the mount is on the clock —
  // the scope is built before it and the teardown runs after it, both outside — so this figure is
  // construction and nothing else. `measureUnmount` below owns the other half. Same op the CLI benches
  // with happy-dom.
  function measureMount(mount, scope) {
    for (let i = 0; i < WARMUP; i++) mount(document.createElement("div"), scope())()
    let iters = 0
    let totalMs = 0
    const budget = benchBudget(BUDGET)
    do {
      const host = document.createElement("div")
      const built = scope()
      const t0 = performance.now()
      const cleanup = mount(host, built)
      totalMs += performance.now() - t0
      iters++
      cleanup()
    } while (budget.more(totalMs * 1e6, iters))
    return { nsPerOp: (totalMs * 1e6) / iters, iters }
  }

  // Teardown, timed on its own — disposing every effect and removing every node the mount built. It
  // used to be folded into `measureMount` (one op did both), which hid it completely: it is a real
  // cost with its own failure modes, and it is what per-item DOM bookkeeping moves. The mount above
  // now excludes it, and builds the scope outside the clock too, so both figures are the op and
  // nothing else. Mirrors the CLI runner's `benchMount`/`benchUnmount` split.
  function measureUnmount(mount, scope) {
    for (let i = 0; i < WARMUP; i++) mount(document.createElement("div"), scope())()
    let iters = 0
    let totalMs = 0
    const budget = benchBudget(BUDGET)
    do {
      const cleanup = mount(document.createElement("div"), scope())
      const t0 = performance.now()
      cleanup()
      totalMs += performance.now() - t0
      iters++
    } while (budget.more(totalMs * 1e6, iters))
    return { nsPerOp: (totalMs * 1e6) / iters, iters }
  }

  // Hydrate timing (browser). Parse the server-rendered HTML ONCE into a template, then time a batch of
  // pristine clones — cloning happens OUTSIDE the timed span (so the parse/clone cost never pollutes the
  // mean), and only `hydrate` is timed: attaching listeners + adopting the existing nodes over the SSR
  // hydration anchors. This is the real first-load flow (the browser already parsed the SSR markup;
  // hydrate only wires it). Unlike mount/update, we can't re-run a fresh op cheaply (each needs its own
  // pristine clone), so instead of an open-ended time loop we CALIBRATE on one hydrate and size a single
  // batch to ~20ms of work — one clock-pair over `batch` ops blunts the coarse clock while keeping the
  // clone count (and memory) bounded regardless of how fast a scenario hydrates.
  function measureHydrate(hydrate, html, scope) {
    const template = document.createElement("div")
    template.innerHTML = html
    for (let i = 0; i < WARMUP; i++) hydrate(template.cloneNode(true), scope())()

    const probe = template.cloneNode(true)
    const p0 = performance.now()
    const probeCleanup = hydrate(probe, scope())
    const oneNs = Math.max(1, (performance.now() - p0) * 1e6)
    probeCleanup()
    const batch = Math.max(5, Math.min(2000, Math.ceil(20e6 / oneNs)))

    const clones = []
    const scopes = []
    for (let k = 0; k < batch; k++) {
      clones.push(template.cloneNode(true))
      scopes.push(scope())
    }
    const cleanups = []
    const t0 = performance.now()
    for (let k = 0; k < batch; k++) cleanups.push(hydrate(clones[k], scopes[k]))
    const elapsedMs = performance.now() - t0
    for (const cleanup of cleanups) cleanup()
    return { nsPerOp: (elapsedMs * 1e6) / batch, iters: batch }
  }

  // HTML parse timing (browser) — the first-load cost that is neither `render` nor `hydrate`: the browser
  // turning served markup into nodes. `measureHydrate` deliberately keeps it off its clock (a hydrate
  // figure should be the anchor walk and nothing else), which is exactly why it has to be measured
  // somewhere: a first-load total that omits it is not a first load, and adopt-vs-build is not a fair
  // comparison without it, since building the DOM by hand parses no markup at all. Timed for BOTH sides'
  // markup — abide's carries hydration anchor comments the hand-written string does not, so parsing them
  // is not the same op. A fresh detached host per iteration: nothing is reused and no layout is triggered.
  // Batched on one clock pair for the same reason `measureHydrate` is, and it is not a nicety here: every
  // op needs a PRISTINE host, so a per-iteration clock pair is the only alternative — and at a sub-µs
  // parse that reads the clock's own resolution rather than the parse. Timed per-op, `interpolation`'s
  // 40 bytes of markup measured 2.84µs, more than `deep-tree-10`'s ten nested elements, and every ratio
  // built on it was inflated by the floor. Calibrate on one parse, size a batch to ~20ms, allocate the
  // hosts OUTSIDE the span so only the parse is on the clock.
  function measureParse(html) {
    for (let i = 0; i < WARMUP; i++) document.createElement("div").innerHTML = html

    const probe = document.createElement("div")
    const p0 = performance.now()
    probe.innerHTML = html
    const oneNs = Math.max(1, (performance.now() - p0) * 1e6)
    const batch = Math.max(5, Math.min(2000, Math.ceil(20e6 / oneNs)))

    const hosts = []
    for (let k = 0; k < batch; k++) hosts.push(document.createElement("div"))
    const t0 = performance.now()
    for (let k = 0; k < batch; k++) hosts[k].innerHTML = html
    const elapsedMs = performance.now() - t0
    return { nsPerOp: (elapsedMs * 1e6) / batch, iters: batch }
  }

  // Adaptive reactive-update timing (browser). A fresh host is mounted OUTSIDE the timed span each round
  // (so mount cost never pollutes the update mean), then a bounded batch of clicks — each a state change
  // flushed to the DOM — is timed as one clock-pair (÷ batch) to blunt the coarse clock. Mirrors the
  // CLI's `benchUpdate` (click the scenario's `<button>`, await the patch).
  async function measureUpdate(mount, scope) {
    // Warmup round.
    {
      const host = document.createElement("div")
      const cleanup = mount(host, scope())
      await flush()
      const button = host.querySelector("button")
      for (let i = 0; i < WARMUP; i++) {
        button?.click()
        await flush()
      }
      cleanup()
    }
    let iters = 0
    let totalMs = 0
    const budget = benchBudget(BUDGET)
    do {
      const host = document.createElement("div")
      const cleanup = mount(host, scope())
      await flush()
      const button = host.querySelector("button")
      const t0 = performance.now()
      for (let i = 0; i < UPDATES_PER_ROUND; i++) {
        button?.click()
        await flush()
      }
      totalMs += performance.now() - t0
      iters += UPDATES_PER_ROUND
      cleanup()
    } while (budget.more(totalMs * 1e6, iters))
    return { nsPerOp: (totalMs * 1e6) / iters, iters }
  }

<script>
  let mountRows = state([])
  let unmountRows = state([])
  let hydrateRows = state([])
  let updateRows = state([])
  // Derived tables: adopt-vs-build (both halves measured in this tab) and the whole first load (the
  // server's render joined to them).
  let buildAdoptRows = state([])
  let firstLoadRows = state([])
  let running = state(false)
  let failed = state(false)

  // Fetch the AOT-bundled corpus, blob-import it as a real ES module, and time the browser hot paths:
  // `mount` (build the DOM) over the pure-render scenarios, then reactive `update` (patch the DOM) over
  // the interactive ones. Rows stream into their tables one scenario at a time (a paint yield between).
  // The last two tables are DERIVED — adopt-vs-build joins figures the passes below already produced, and
  // first-load joins them to the server's own `render` bench, drained over the wire at the very end.
  async function run() {
    if (running) return
    running = true
    failed = false
    mountRows = []
    unmountRows = []
    hydrateRows = []
    updateRows = []
    buildAdoptRows = []
    firstLoadRows = []
    try {
      const bundle = await benchFrontendClient()
      const url = URL.createObjectURL(new Blob([bundle.js], { type: "text/javascript" }))
      let mod
      try {
        mod = await import(/* @vite-ignore */ url)
      } finally {
        URL.revokeObjectURL(url)
      }
      const scopes = scopesFor(mod)
      const scopeFor = (name) => scopes.find((s) => s.name === name)?.scope

      // Mount pass — build the DOM from scratch (the pure-render corpus). Each scenario is timed twice,
      // back to back: abide's `mount`, then the hand-written equivalent that builds the same DOM with
      // plain `createElement` calls. In a real browser that second number is what the DOM itself costs,
      // so the ratio is the only part of the figure that is actually abide.
      const mounts = []
      for (const scenario of bundle.scenarios) {
        if (scenario.update) continue
        const entry = mod.scenarios[scenario.name]
        const scope = scopeFor(scenario.name)
        // LOUD, not skipped. `scopesFor` is hand-maintained against the shared corpus, so a scenario
        // added there but not here would otherwise vanish from this page with no error at all — the
        // bench would quietly measure less than it claims to.
        if (entry === undefined || scope === undefined)
          throw new Error("bench scenario has no compiled entry or client scope, add it to scopesFor — " + scenario.name)
        const { nsPerOp, iters } = measureMount(entry.mount, scope)
        const baseline = mod.VANILLA_BASELINES[scenario.name]
        const vanilla = baseline ? measureMount(baseline.mount, scope) : null
        mounts.push({
          name: scenario.name,
          nsPerOp,
          iters,
          rows: scenario.rows,
          nsPerRow: scenario.rows ? nsPerOp / scenario.rows : null,
          vanillaNsPerOp: vanilla ? vanilla.nsPerOp : null,
          vanillaNote: baseline ? baseline.note : null,
          ratio: vanilla ? nsPerOp / vanilla.nsPerOp : null,
        })
        mountRows = [...mounts]
        await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 0))
      }

      // Unmount pass — teardown on its own clock, over the same pure-render corpus. The hand-written
      // baseline here is `host.replaceChildren()`, ONE engine call, which a framework tracking
      // per-item disposers structurally cannot match; read this ratio as a regression guard and a
      // pointer at per-item bookkeeping, not as a like-for-like overhead figure.
      const unmounts = []
      for (const scenario of bundle.scenarios) {
        if (scenario.update) continue
        const entry = mod.scenarios[scenario.name]
        const scope = scopeFor(scenario.name)
        if (entry === undefined || scope === undefined)
          throw new Error("bench scenario has no compiled entry or client scope, add it to scopesFor — " + scenario.name)
        const { nsPerOp, iters } = measureUnmount(entry.mount, scope)
        const baseline = mod.VANILLA_BASELINES[scenario.name]
        const vanilla = baseline ? measureUnmount(baseline.mount, scope) : null
        unmounts.push({
          name: scenario.name,
          nsPerOp,
          iters,
          rows: scenario.rows,
          nsPerRow: scenario.rows ? nsPerOp / scenario.rows : null,
          vanillaNsPerOp: vanilla ? vanilla.nsPerOp : null,
          vanillaNote: baseline ? baseline.note : null,
          ratio: vanilla ? nsPerOp / vanilla.nsPerOp : null,
        })
        unmountRows = [...unmounts]
        await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 0))
      }

      // Hydrate pass — attach to server-rendered HTML (first-load interactivity). Alongside the walk it
      // times the browser's PARSE of both sides' markup (abide's anchored SSR output, and the baseline's
      // hand-concatenated string built right here from the same scope) — the two figures the derived
      // tables below are missing, and the reason each of them can carry a vanilla column at all.
      const hydrates = []
      for (const scenario of bundle.scenarios) {
        if (scenario.html === null) continue
        const entry = mod.scenarios[scenario.name]
        const scope = scopeFor(scenario.name)
        // LOUD, not skipped. `scopesFor` is hand-maintained against the shared corpus, so a scenario
        // added there but not here would otherwise vanish from this page with no error at all — the
        // bench would quietly measure less than it claims to.
        if (entry === undefined || scope === undefined)
          throw new Error("bench scenario has no compiled entry or client scope, add it to scopesFor — " + scenario.name)
        const { nsPerOp, iters } = measureHydrate(entry.hydrate, scenario.html, scope)
        const parse = measureParse(scenario.html)
        const baseline = mod.VANILLA_BASELINES[scenario.name]
        const vanillaHtml = baseline && baseline.render ? await baseline.render(scope()) : null
        const vanillaParse = vanillaHtml === null ? null : measureParse(vanillaHtml)
        hydrates.push({
          name: scenario.name,
          nsPerOp,
          iters,
          rows: scenario.rows,
          nsPerRow: scenario.rows ? nsPerOp / scenario.rows : null,
          parseNsPerOp: parse.nsPerOp,
          vanillaParseNsPerOp: vanillaParse ? vanillaParse.nsPerOp : null,
        })
        hydrateRows = [...hydrates]

        // Derived, measured nowhere new: the same scenario's `mount` figure from the pass above, next to
        // the adopt path. Two ratios, because there are two questions. `hydrate ÷ mount` is abide against
        // itself — is adopting cheaper than building? — and both numbers came out of this tab minutes
        // apart, so it is the clean one. `adopt ÷ vanilla build` is the STRATEGY comparison, and the
        // closest thing hydrate has to a hand-written baseline: ship SSR markup and walk it, versus ship
        // none and build the DOM with `createElement`. It is honest only because `parse` is in the
        // numerator — the adopt path pays for markup the build path never sends.
        const mounted = mounts.find((m) => m.name === scenario.name)
        if (mounted === undefined)
          throw new Error("hydrated a scenario the mount pass never measured — the two corpora have drifted: " + scenario.name)
        const adoptNsPerOp = parse.nsPerOp + nsPerOp
        buildAdoptRows = [
          ...buildAdoptRows,
          {
            name: scenario.name,
            mountNsPerOp: mounted.nsPerOp,
            hydrateNsPerOp: nsPerOp,
            parseNsPerOp: parse.nsPerOp,
            adoptNsPerOp,
            hydrateOverMount: nsPerOp / mounted.nsPerOp,
            adoptOverVanillaBuild: mounted.vanillaNsPerOp === null ? null : adoptNsPerOp / mounted.vanillaNsPerOp,
          },
        ]
        await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 0))
      }

      // Update pass — the interactive corpus (reactive patch cost). The vanilla baseline mounts its own
      // `<button>` wired to a direct DOM write, so the SAME click-and-flush loop times both sides.
      const updates = []
      for (const scenario of bundle.scenarios) {
        if (!scenario.update) continue
        const entry = mod.scenarios[scenario.name]
        const scope = scopeFor(scenario.name)
        // LOUD, not skipped. `scopesFor` is hand-maintained against the shared corpus, so a scenario
        // added there but not here would otherwise vanish from this page with no error at all — the
        // bench would quietly measure less than it claims to.
        if (entry === undefined || scope === undefined)
          throw new Error("bench scenario has no compiled entry or client scope, add it to scopesFor — " + scenario.name)
        const { nsPerOp, iters } = await measureUpdate(entry.mount, scope)
        const baseline = mod.VANILLA_BASELINES[scenario.name]
        const vanilla = baseline ? await measureUpdate(baseline.mount, scope) : null
        updates.push({
          name: scenario.name,
          nsPerOp,
          iters,
          vanillaNsPerOp: vanilla ? vanilla.nsPerOp : null,
          vanillaNote: baseline ? baseline.note : null,
          ratio: vanilla ? nsPerOp / vanilla.nsPerOp : null,
        })
        updateRows = [...updates]
        await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 0))
      }

      // First-load pass — the one half of a first paint this tab cannot time itself: the server's
      // `render`. Rather than a second copy of that loop, it drains the SAME streaming rpc the
      // /platform/bench page drives (abide's render and the baseline's string concat, both timed on the
      // server) and joins each row to the parse + hydrate figures measured above by scenario name. Runs
      // LAST on purpose: an in-flight fetch resolving inside a timed batch is jitter, and every browser
      // figure it needs is already collected by here.
      //
      // `invalidate` first because the browser memo is a tab-lifetime cache: without it a second click
      // would replay the FIRST run's transcript and pair stale render numbers with fresh hydrate ones.
      benchFrontend.invalidate()
      const firstLoads = []
      // A streaming rpc resolves to its cursor, so the call is awaited before the drain (in a template a
      // `{#for await}` opener does this for you; a `<script>` is plain JS and does not).
      const renderRows = await benchFrontend()
      for await (const row of renderRows) {
        const hydrated = hydrates.find((h) => h.name === row.name)
        // Both corpora are filtered by the same `server !== false` predicate, so a name in one and not the
        // other is real drift, not a scenario that opted out.
        if (hydrated === undefined)
          throw new Error("the render corpus timed a scenario the hydrate pass never saw — the two have drifted: " + row.name)
        const totalNsPerOp = row.nsPerOp + hydrated.parseNsPerOp + hydrated.nsPerOp
        // The hand-written first load: its own string build, then the browser parsing ITS markup (no
        // anchors), and then nothing — an inert page has no bindings to wire.
        const vanillaTotalNsPerOp =
          row.vanillaNsPerOp === null || hydrated.vanillaParseNsPerOp === null
            ? null
            : row.vanillaNsPerOp + hydrated.vanillaParseNsPerOp
        firstLoads.push({
          name: row.name,
          renderNsPerOp: row.nsPerOp,
          parseNsPerOp: hydrated.parseNsPerOp,
          hydrateNsPerOp: hydrated.nsPerOp,
          totalNsPerOp,
          vanillaTotalNsPerOp,
          ratio: vanillaTotalNsPerOp === null ? null : totalNsPerOp / vanillaTotalNsPerOp,
          nearFloor: row.nearFloor,
        })
        firstLoadRows = [...firstLoads]
      }
    } catch {
      failed = true
    } finally {
      running = false
    }
  }

CLI

One binary, abide, drives the whole lifecycle — scaffold, develop, type-check, build, serve, and package. Every command runs the SAME Bun pipeline (no divergent dev runtime), so what you see in abide dev is what ships.

abide scaffold my-app
  # writes a starter project, then: git init + bun install + abide dev
  # skip any step: --no-git / --no-install / --no-dev

scaffold writes a minimal, representative starter — one type-derived RPC, one page reading it, the middleware/lifecycle module, a config stub — then runs git init, bun install, and abide dev for you.

abide dev            # watch + rebuild + full live-reload (over the socket mux)
  abide dev --port 4321

dev serves the app with a filesystem watch: on any change it rebuilds (Bun is fast) and signals a live-reload over the socket mux — a fast full reload, not stateful HMR (which would be a runtime that diverges from production).

abide check           # type-check .abide (template + cross-file component props)
  abide lsp             # .abide language server over stdio (editors)

check type-checks .abide files — script bodies, template expressions, and cross-file component props — by lowering to TypeScript and mapping diagnostics back. lsp exposes the same engine to editors (diagnostics, hover, go-to-definition, completion, signature help, references, and semantic-token highlighting) — the packages/zed-abide extension runs it in Zed.

abide build          # code-split client → dist/_app/<hash>/

build produces the production client: a code-split, content-hashed bundle written to dist/_app/<hash>/ with a stable manifest.json pointer. See Build & deploy for the output layout and how start serves it.

abide start          # serve the built dist (no bundler at boot)
  abide start --port 8080

start serves the artifacts build produced — no bundler runs at boot. If no build exists yet, it builds once, then serves.

abide run scripts/seed.ts arg1 arg2
  # runs under the abide runtime (no HTTP; onStart / onStop still fire)

run executes a one-off script under the abide runtime — no HTTP server, but the app's onStart/onStop lifecycle hooks fire, so migrations and seeds get the same environment as the server.

# inside the binary's REPL, TAB already completes — nothing to install
  eval "$(./myapp completion bash)"     # bash
  eval "$(./myapp completion zsh)"      # zsh
  ./myapp completion fish | source      # fish

As you type at the prompt, dim ghost text appears inline: the best match where you are completing one, and once you have named a command, its whole signature — --name <string> --loud, with a boolean carrying no placeholder and an enum showing its set. Press → (or ctrl-e) at the end of the line to accept the flag itself, or keep typing to ignore it; it is never part of the line you submit, and it is suppressed under NO_COLOR. TAB completes command names, the reserved built-ins, a command's --flags, and a field's enum values — all read from your input schemas, so there is no completion list to maintain beside your handlers. The generated shell script does not bake those names in: it calls myapp completion --line "<line>" on every TAB, which is the same call the REPL makes, so the shell and the prompt can never offer different candidates and neither goes stale when a handler gains a field. Completing a command boots nothing.

abide compile --target bun-linux-x64 --out ./server
  abide compile --platforms bun-linux-x64,bun-darwin-arm64
  # ONE executable: it hosts the app, dispatches your rpcs as subcommands,
  # and runs interactive — you pick when you RUN it, not when you build it
  
  abide bundle         # desktop launcher (host platform; embeds assets)

compile emits a single self-contained executable (app + client assets embedded, no external dist/) — hosting it takes --port and PORT like abide start, and defaults its output to dist/<app name>. Everything the server would otherwise look up at runtime is resolved at build time: your rpc/socket/app.ts modules become static imports, and every page, layout and component is compiled to its server module ahead of time. The one thing a binary cannot carry is your SOURCE — a module that reads paths off import.meta.dir won't find them. There is no separate CLI build — the same executable is your command-line tool. --platforms cross-compiles a release set for the price of one client build. bundle builds a desktop launcher.

./myapp                        # interactive, schema-driven prompts (the default)
  ./myapp hello --who cli        # one rpc → JSON on stdout
  ./myapp help hello             # flags, typed from the input schema
  ./myapp serve --port 8080      # host the app in the foreground
  > serve --port 8080            # …or from inside a session

  ./myapp connect https://app.example.com --token $TOKEN
  ./myapp hello --who remote     # …every later run goes there
  ./myapp disconnect             # …until you hand the app back

  ./myapp --url https://staging.example.com hello   # one run, somewhere else

  ./myapp login --token $TOKEN   # remember WHO you are there
  ./myapp identity               # …and ask the server who it thinks you are
  ./myapp logs --tail 200        # live log feed from wherever you point
  ./myapp logs --debug abide:rpc --trace 4bf92f35

logs tails a deployment's log records as they happen. Filters are applied on the server: --tail <n> replays backlog before going live (200 by default), --level <l> sets a severity floor, --debug <pattern> takes the same grammar DEBUG uses, --trace <id> matches a trace-id prefix so the 8 hex a pretty line prints is paste-able, and --no-follow prints history then exits. Records arrive structured and are rendered by the READER, through the same formatter the server uses for its own stdout — so a remote tail at your terminal looks exactly like reading that server's console, and through a pipe degrades to the same tsv. At the prompt, ctrl-c detaches the feed instead of ending the session.

It needs ABIDE_LOGS set on the server, and is a 404 otherwise. That default is deliberate: every other generated route discloses something the caller already holds, and this one discloses whatever your app logged — including lines written on behalf of other users. It is served inside your middleware chain, so authorization is your own middleware, the same answer abide gives everywhere else. Because the fan-out happens before the DEBUG gate, logs --debug abide:rpc can light a framework channel on a live deployment that was booted without it, which is the thing that makes a remote feed worth having.

The executable IS your app. Every rpc reachable by clients.cli becomes a subcommand, and its input schema becomes the flags — so --n 5 on an integer field arrives as the number 5, and --help knows the types without asking a server. Results are JSON on stdout (pretty at a terminal, compact through a pipe), a streaming handler is line-streamed as it arrives, and failures are a JSON object on stderr plus an exit code that names the failure class — 2 for a bad command line, 3 for a 422, 4 for 401/403, 7 for a 5xx.

Where a call lands is a four-rung ladder: --url for this run, then ABIDE_APP_URL for this environment, then whatever connect stored for this user, and otherwise the app itself. Flag over environment over stored file, so ABIDE_APP_URL=… ./myapp beats a connected binary without disconnecting it first. connect keeps its target in your per-user data directory (mode 0600 — it may hold a bearer), which is why it survives between runs and follows you between directories; bare connect tells you where you are pointed, and both commands work from the prompt too.

With nothing pointing it anywhere, it hosts its OWN copy of the app on a loopback port and calls that — offline, self-sufficient, and over real HTTP, so your middleware, identity, validation and caching behave exactly as they do in production. Hosting is lazy: printing help or mistyping a command never runs your onStart. With a URL it calls that deployment instead, authenticating with --token / ABIDE_APP_TOKEN; the embedded app still supplies the command table, so the CLI knows every flag even when the deployment is unreachable.

Because the command surface is the DEFAULT, a deployment has to say serve — an entrypoint that omits it starts an interactive session with no console, which the binary reports as an error rather than exiting quietly.

Nine names are reserved and win over an rpc of the same name: serve, connect, disconnect, login, logout, identity, logs, help and completion. All nine are answered on both surfaces — on a command line and at the prompt. That is a guarantee now rather than a coincidence: one table carries each name's where, and both surfaces dispatch through it exhaustively, so a reserved name no surface answers does not compile. completion was exactly that gap — listed in help, warned about as shadowing your rpc, and answered unknown command at the prompt. For serve the reason is rescue — hosting has no second door — but the rest are the binary's operational vocabulary about a deployment rather than calls into your app, and a reserved list you have to memorise exceptions to is worse than one shadowed rpc. Two more, exit and quit, are reserved at the prompt only: they end a session, which means nothing on a command line, so an rpc named exit is still callable as ./myapp exit and is merely unreachable from the REPL. A shadowed rpc still appears in help, still runs over HTTP, MCP and the browser, and warns on the abide:cli channel naming which of the two you lost — or set clients.cli: false to drop it from this surface deliberately.

Config

env(schema) reads typed, boot-validated config from the environment. Strings are coerced by the schema ("25" → number, "true" → boolean), schema defaults fill missing keys, and it fails fast if a required var is missing or invalid. Below is a live read of an env()-backed RPC.

A one-shot read of an env()-backed GET. The await blocks SSR, so the coerced, schema-defaulted values land in the initial HTML; "Run again" refreshes the cached read.

VariableEffect

APP_URLPublic app URL → the mount base, and the allowed Origin for the CSRF check.
ABIDE_DATA_DIRPer-user data directory (backs appDataDir()).
ABIDE_IDENTITY_SECRETRequired in production. Seals the abide-identity cookie + tokens so authenticated identity.set() survives restarts and is stable across instances.
ABIDE_IDENTITY_TTLIdentity cookie/token TTL in ms (default 30 days, rolling).

It is served inside your middleware chain, so authorization is your own middleware.
ABIDE_LOG_BUFFERSize of that feed's backlog ring, in records (default 500). It fills unconditionally once the feed is enabled — you run logs after noticing a problem, and a feed that starts empty at connect has discarded the only lines you wanted.

Beyond your own env() schema, abide reads these built-in variables from the environment. Set them in your process manager or container (see Build & deploy). The one production requirement is ABIDE_IDENTITY_SECRET — without it, authenticated identity does not survive a restart.
src/ui/pages/platform/deploy/page.abide:
Build & deploy

Deploying is two steps: abide build writes a content-addressed client into dist/, and abide start serves it. Production runs no bundler — start reads the built artifacts and serves them with immutable long-cache headers.

abide build

The client is code-split per route: one loader entry, one chunk per page.abide (with its layouts folded in), and shared chunks for the runtime and shared layouts/components. Every file name embeds a content hash, so it is safe to cache forever.

dist/
  ├─ manifest.json                 # stable pointer → the current build
  └─ _app/
     └─ <hash>/
        ├─ index.json              # hash, entry, css, files, chunkByPattern
        ├─ loader-<hash>.js        # the boot entry the document loads
        ├─ chain-0-index-<hash>.js # one code-split chunk per route
        ├─ chunk-<hash>.js         # shared chunks (runtime, layouts …)
        └─ style-<hash>.css        # bundled + hashed stylesheet

The output is deterministic — the same source yields the same hashes (reproducible builds, CDN-friendly):

ABIDE_IDENTITY_SECRET=… PORT=8080 abide start

abide start loads dist/manifest.json, serves each hashed file under /__abide/chunk/, and boots the document from the hashed loader — no bundler at request or boot time. (If no build is present it builds once, then serves, so start always works.)

GET /__abide/chunk/chain-0-index-a1b2c3d4.js
  → 200  cache-control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable

Because every asset URL is content-addressed, the response is immutable — a client caches it once and never revalidates until a new build changes the hash:

The first load fetches only the matched route's chunk plus the shared runtime; other routes load lazily on soft-nav. SSR still renders every page server-side — the build artifacts are the browser JS, not the server render.

The document's <head> modulepreloads that whole boot graph — the loader entry, its transitive static imports, then the route's chunk and its static imports, each named individually. The executing <script> has to stay last, since it must not run before the hydration seed is parsed, which meant the browser did not discover the client bundle until the last byte — after every streamed read had drained. On this app that was a boot download starting at 4494ms on a page whose first byte arrived at 364ms; with the links the whole graph is down by 392ms while the document streams on. Naming only the entry is not enough: following a preloaded module's own static imports is optional in the HTML spec and Safari declines, so it moves the waterfall down one level instead of removing it. Only static edges are followed — the dynamic ones are the other routes, and preloading those would fetch the whole app on every page.

Production configuration is environment variables, validated at boot via env(). At minimum set ABIDE_IDENTITY_SECRET (seals the identity cookie + tokens so authenticated identity survives restarts) and PORT. The full list of abide's built-in variables lives on the Config page.

 
abide compile --target bun-linux-x64 --out ./server
  ./server serve                 # runs anywhere — app + assets embedded, no dist/

For deploys without a Bun runtime on the host, abide compile emits a single executable with the app and client assets embedded — no external dist/, nothing to install. The serve subcommand is what hosts it — the same executable also dispatches your rpcs as subcommands and opens an interactive session, so spell it in an entrypoint. It takes --port and PORT like abide start, and shuts down through onStop on SIGTERM. The trade is that the binary carries no source tree: a module that reads or resolves its own files at runtime (via import.meta.dir) has nothing to find, so do that work on first call rather than at import.

docker build -t deploy .
  docker run -p 8080:8080 -e ABIDE_IDENTITY_SECRET=… deploy

Two shapes, same workflow — build and run either with the deploy tag:

FROM oven/bun:1 AS build
  WORKDIR /app
  COPY . .
  RUN bun install --frozen-lockfile && bun run abide build
  
  FROM oven/bun:1
  WORKDIR /app
  COPY --from=build /app /app
  ENV PORT=8080
  ENV ABIDE_IDENTITY_SECRET=change-me
  EXPOSE 8080
  CMD ["bun", "run", "abide", "start"]

A two-stage image: build the client, then serve it. The runtime stage carries the app plus its dist/ and runs under Bun.

FROM oven/bun:1 AS build
  WORKDIR /app
  COPY . .
  RUN bun install --frozen-lockfile && bun run abide compile --target bun-linux-x64 --out ./server
  
  FROM debian:bookworm-slim
  COPY --from=build /app/server /usr/local/bin/server
  ENV PORT=8080
  ENV ABIDE_IDENTITY_SECRET=change-me
  EXPOSE 8080
  ENTRYPOINT ["server", "serve"]

Compile one self-contained executable — it embeds Bun, the app, and the client assets — and drop it into a minimal base image. No Bun, no dist/, nothing else in the runtime layer.
src/ui/pages/platform/identity/page.abid:
Identity

identity() is the current principal — never null, and isomorphic: the same import answers in a handler and in a component, where it returns what the server resolved for this page (seeded at hydration, reactive). It starts anonymous; identity.set() promotes it and the router seals a rolling cookie so it persists across requests. A browser cannot seal a cookie, so it cannot promote itself — identity.refresh() re-asks the server after a login mutation. Log in, then watch BOTH lines flip.

The principal in one loop. The read calls identity(); login() is a mutation that calls identity.set() server-side, and re-reading over a fresh request — now carrying the sealed abide-identity cookie — proves the authenticated principal survived the round trip. logout() puts it back to anonymous.
src/ui/pages/platform/lifecycle/page.abi:
Lifecycle hooks

src/app.ts exports four lifecycle hooks alongside the middleware onion. onStart(start) and onStop(stop) wrap the real boot/teardown; onHealth() and onError() run per request, inside request scope. The server tab of each card shows this app's real source.

onStart(start) runs setup and then await start() to bind the server — the socket binds only inside start(), so nothing serves until setup finishes (returning without calling it aborts boot). Here it seeds a bootId before booting. onHealth() then runs on every GET /__abide/health and merges its fields over the framework stub of reachable, version, startedAt, and uptime — the app + bootId fields below prove both hooks ran. Return reachable: false (or throw) and the endpoint answers 503. onStop(stop) (also in the app.ts source) mirrors onStart for graceful shutdown — no live UI effect.

health() is isomorphic, so this fetches the live /__abide/health and shows the merged document: the framework stub (reachable, version, startedAt, uptime) plus what onHealth() merged over it. A non-empty bootId is the proof that onStart ran and seeded it before the server bound.

The RPC below throws an unexpected error — not a typed error(), which also throws but is rendered at its own status before the hook. onError(error) (request-scoped) catches it and returns the Response the client sees, instead of an opaque crash. The button posts to it and shows the shaped status + message.

An RPC that throws. .raw() bypasses the memo and returns the untouched Response, so what you see is exactly the status and body onError shaped — a typed error() would never reach the hook. Not because it isn't a throw (it is one), but because it throws an HttpError, which the router renders at the status the handler asked for before the hook is consulted: a declared 404 is not a bug in the app.
src/ui/pages/platform/machines/page.abid:
Machine surfaces

Every RPC is automatically a machine surface — no second implementation. One handler is a browser fetch, an OpenAPI operation, and an MCP tool at once. Fetch each surface live from this browser page and render what a machine would see.

  • /openapi.json — an OpenAPI 3.1 document describing every RPC.
  • /__abide/mcp — a Model Context Protocol endpoint exposing RPCs as tools.
  • /__abide/rpc/<name> — each RPC's own transport, plus ?__abide_from=<n> to resume a retained stream.
  • /__abide/sockets — the multiplexed WebSocket, and a per-socket HTTP face.
  • /__abide/health — reachability and whatever onHealth() merges in.
  • /__abide/identity — the caller's OWN resolved principal; it discloses nothing they do not already hold.
  • /__abide/logs — a live SSE log feed. The one generated route that is off by default (ABIDE_LOGS), because it is the one that discloses something the caller did not already have.

All of them run through your middleware chain, like every other route — which is the whole authorization story for each of them.

Nothing here was written by hand. Both documents here are generated from the same RPC definitions the browser calls, which is why they cannot drift from the implementation — there is only one.

And so does a tool call. An MCP tools/call, and an agent() run reaching for one of these same RPCs, both dispatch over this app's own HTTP face on the loopback rather than invoking the handler in-process. That is not a detour, and the reason is narrower than it looks: the arguments were written by a model, so they are untrusted input. An RPC's schemas.input validation is composed by the router, so an in-process call would advertise the declared schema to the model and never enforce what it sent back. (Its middleware is no longer part of that argument — that runs per read, from whichever door the read came through, this page's own SSR included.) For a caller choosing what to invoke, with arguments it wrote itself, that is the difference between "reachability, not authorization" and no authorization at all. One loopback request means the whole chain applies verbatim — CSRF, CORS, identity, middleware, input validation, the memo, the run deadline — with no second copy of any of it. The call inherits the identity of whatever provoked it (the incoming MCP request, or the request scope an agent() run sits inside); from a cron tick or an abide run script it goes out anonymous, which is the fail-closed answer.

Fetched from this browser page: the generated OpenAPI 3.1 document, rendered as its operation paths. Every RPC is projected as an operation — there is no second implementation to keep in step.

The same handlers again, this time over JSON-RPC 2.0: a tools/list call to /__abide/mcp, rendered as tool names. An RPC reaches this surface when clients.mcp admits it.

The surfaces above are only useful because the app's capabilities are data. This list is read from the same capabilities RPC an agent would call over MCP — one GET handler that a browser, an OpenAPI operation, and an MCP tool all share.

A description is only half of it — something has to call these tools. That is an agent: the same RPCs and schemas, now driven by a model. agent(engine, messages, options) drives any AgentEngine (the shipped Claude / Claude Code engines, or a scripted one). Here a deterministic scripted engine requests the clock tool; the loop calls it back through this app's own HTTP face — so the rpc's middleware and input validation run on the model's arguments — and streams every AgentFrame, consumed live with {'{'}#for await{'}'}. The tool set defaults to the app's clients.mcp RPCs: an rpc withheld from MCP is withheld here too, by the same declaration.
src/ui/pages/platform/observability/page:
Observability

Four questions an app asks about itself, in increasing depth: where am I running, is the server healthy, what happened during this request, and what should I record. Each has one import and no plumbing.

online() is a reactive connectivity boolean (true on the server; tracks navigator.onLine on the client, so this line re-renders when you go offline). Imported straight from abide/shared/online and called in the template — no RPC, no accessor plumbing.

The cheapest probes: two booleans, imported and called straight in a template. online() is reactive — it tracks navigator.onLine, so the line here re-renders when you go offline (and is simply true on the server).

bundled() is true only inside the desktop bundle, false in the browser. Imported straight from abide/ui/bundled and called in the template.

bundled() is true only inside the desktop bundle, false in a browser — the other one-import probe, called straight in the template.

Same shape, one step out: health() is isomorphic, and the document is the same on both sides — composed in-process on the server, fetched from /__abide/health in the browser. App fields from onHealth() merge over the baseline either way, and their TYPES come from a generated src/.abide/health.d.ts, so (await health()).bootId is a typed read in this app and a compile error in one with no such hook. The second line proves it rather than asserting it: the server tab is an RPC that calls the same health() and reads doc.bootId straight off the document, where the checker is real. The browser half above cannot — it holds the document in a cell that widens to any, so nothing there consults the generated companion.

trace() returns the request's W3C traceparent — the id that ties this request to whatever called it, and to whatever it calls next. The router echoes it back on the response, so a trace crosses the boundary without you threading anything.

Every request gets a traceparent whether or not a handler asks: the router propagates a well-formed incoming one and otherwise mints one, so every response carries traceparent + traceresponse. (The one exception is a content-addressed /__abide/chunk/ asset — immutable, identity-free, joined by no span.)

trace() is isomorphic, so it answers in the browser too — with the id of the request that rendered the live page, re-adopted on every navigation. The client never mints one: an id generated in a tab would name a trace no server span belongs to.

A browser RPC call carries it as a CHILD span — same trace id, fresh span id, which is what W3C asks of a caller — so the handler's work joins the page's trace. Click Run again above and the traceId holds while the span half moves. A navigation deliberately carries nothing: a nav is a new operation, and propagating would grow one immortal trace per tab.

log is isomorphic structured logging. Every line carries a channel label. The bare log() / .info / .warn / .error / .trace uses the default channel — the app name (docs here, from package.json) — and is always on. log.channel(name) names a channel gated by DEBUG (debug-npm style; the browser reads localStorage.debug), so framework internals under abide:* and verbose app channels stay quiet until asked for. A bare name is namespaced under the app for you — channel('cards') labels and gates as docs:cards, and DEBUG=docs:* lights every channel this app owns. error always emits, even on a gated channel. This RPC logs server-side (browser never sees the lines) and returns the fact that it logged:

log() writes on the server, so the card reports what the handler logged rather than showing it: an info line on the always-on default channel (the app name) and a trace line on the DEBUG-gated docs:cards channel. The gated one only reaches your terminal under DEBUG=docs:cards.
