src/ui/pages/platform/scope/page.abide:
Request scope

A handler doesn't take the request as a parameter — it asks for what it needs, ambiently. This page goes in the order the request itself does: read what the client sent, carry your own values alongside it, then wrap the whole thing in middleware that can stop it.

cookies() reads the request cookie jar. The browser sets document.cookie, then the RPC reads it back server-side — the value round-trips through the request scope.

Cookies come from the client; context() is the same idea for values you put on the request. It is the per-request carrier bag. A per-RPC middleware writes into it; the handler beneath it in the onion reads it back — the hand-off from a middleware layer to the handler.

Note when it ran. The stamp is already filled in before you touch the button, because this page read the RPC during its own server render — and an RPC's middleware runs per read, from every door, not only over HTTP. The button is a second read through the browser, so the middleware runs a second time. That is the whole rule: middleware is (next) => Response, so it is tracing and rate limiting and context-filling as much as it is auth, and a read that skipped it would not merely be unauthorized — it would be unobserved.

Middleware is the layer around a handler — and the reason context() exists, since it is how a layer hands something down. A per-RPC middleware array composes an onion: the first layer authorizes, either calling error(403) to short-circuit (it throws, so the handler never runs and the chain renders the 403) or calling next(). Both buttons hit the real router pipeline in the browser.

There are two rungs, and they differ in how often they run. An RPC's own middleware is per read — every read, every door. Your src/app.ts middleware array is per request: a page with eight reads runs it once, not nine times, which is what keeps a rate limiter honest. From a door with no request at all — a cron tick, an abide run migration — the read still runs its own rung, and the global one stays out of it, because there is no request there for it to authorize.
src/ui/pages/platform/testing/page.abide:
Testing

await createTestApp() boots the real router in-process on an ephemeral port and hands back a tiny surface — no mocks, no divergent runtime. You test against the same request pipeline that ships: middleware, the CSRF gate, identity sealing, cache memos, sockets, and SSR all run for real. It is async — always await it.

How you call it decides what gets registered:

  • Explicit — the config names at least one surface (routes / sockets / pages / layouts / middleware). Only what you name is registered — a hermetic app, no filesystem scan, no lifecycle. The classic unit-test shape.
  • Discovery — the config names no surface (createTestApp(), createTestApp({}), or only the control knobs below). The whole project is loaded from disk — every src/server/rpc/**, socket, page, layout, and src/app.ts middleware — and booted through its onStart/onStop hooks. Integration-test against the real app.
 
import { afterEach, expect, test } from 'bun:test'
  import { GET } from 'abide/server/GET'
  import { POST } from 'abide/server/POST'
  import { createTestApp, type TestApp } from 'abide/test/createTestApp'
  
  const greet = GET(async ({ name }: { name: string }) => ({ greeting: `hello ${name}` }))
  
  let running: TestApp | undefined
  afterEach(async () => {
    await running?.stop()
    running = undefined
  })
  
  test('greet returns a greeting', async () => {
    const app = (running = await createTestApp({ routes: { greet } }))
    expect(app.origin).toMatch(/^http:\/\/localhost:\d+$/)
  })

Name the RPCs (and, optionally, middleware, sockets, pages, and layouts) you want under test. Every call listens on a fresh localhost port, so suites stay isolated. Always stop() it — a throw before teardown can leak the harness into other files.

// whole real app, discovered from cwd, onStart/onStop run
  const app = await createTestApp()
  expect(await app.rpc.greet({ name: 'x' })).toEqual({ greeting: 'hello x' })
  
  // same app from a specific project root, skipping the boot hooks
  const fast = await createTestApp({ dir: './packages/api', lifecycle: false })

Call it with no surface and it loads the entire project from process.cwd() and runs its lifecycle — the same wiring abide start boots, so your test exercises the real middleware, config, and every registered RPC. Point dir at another root for monorepo layouts. When a test doesn't need an expensive boot (a DB pool, migrations), skip the hooks with lifecycle: false — discovery still runs, only onStart/onStop are skipped.

const bump = POST(async ({ by = 1 }: { by?: number }) => ({ total: (counter += by) }))
  
  const app = await createTestApp({ routes: { greet, bump } })
  
  // read — args in the query string
  expect(await app.rpc.greet({ name: 'x' })).toEqual({ greeting: 'hello x' })
  
  // mutation — args in the body, CSRF-admitted
  expect(await app.rpc.bump({ by: 2 })).toEqual({ total: 2 })

The rpc proxy calls a registered route with the right verb and encoding: reads put args in the URL, mutations post JSON in the body with the headers the CSRF gate expects. It returns the decoded JSON payload.

const res = await app.fetch(
    `/__abide/rpc/greet?__abide_args=${encodeURIComponent(JSON.stringify({ name: 'x' }))}`,
  )
  expect(res.status).toBe(200)
  expect(res.headers.get('content-type')).toContain('application/json')
  
  // SSR a page (register it via `pages`) and assert the HTML
  const page = await app.fetch('/')
  expect(await page.text()).toContain('<main')

Drop to fetch(path, init?) against the live origin when you need to assert status codes, headers, or transport details the proxy hides. This is the same Request → Response path the browser hits. Building the URL by hand means naming the reserved transport param yourself: a read's canonical JSON args blob is ?__abide_args=<json> (the __abide_ prefix is what stops it colliding with a handler's own arg field). Flat per-field params — ?name=x — work too, coerced by the input schema.

import { identity } from 'abide/shared/identity'
  
  const whoami = GET(async () => ({ id: identity().id, authenticated: identity().authenticated }))
  const app = await createTestApp({ routes: { whoami } })
  
  expect((await app.rpc.whoami()).authenticated).toBe(false)
  
  const asUser = app.as({ id: 'user-1', authenticated: true })
  expect(await asUser.rpc.whoami()).toEqual({ id: 'user-1', authenticated: true })

app.as(identity) returns a sibling TestApp bound to the same origin that stamps a sealed Authorization: Bearer header onto every request — exercising the real per-user-token rung of the identity ladder. No second server starts, and the base app stays anonymous, so you can compare both in one test.

import { createTestApp, identityCookie } from 'abide/test/createTestApp'
  
  const loginRes = await app.fetch('/__abide/rpc/login', {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json' },
    body: '{}',
  })
  const cookie = identityCookie(loginRes) // "abide-identity=…"
  
  const follow = await app.fetch('/__abide/rpc/whoami?__abide_args=%7B%7D', { headers: { cookie } })
  expect((await follow.json()).authenticated).toBe(true)

To exercise the cookie rung instead of a bearer token, log in through a mutation that calls identity.set(), then read the abide-identity cookie off the response with identityCookie() and replay it on a follow-up request.

const client = app.socket()
  await client.ready()
  
  const messages = client.subscribe<{ text: string }>('chat')
  client.publish('chat', { text: 'hi' })
  
  for await (const msg of messages) {
    expect(msg.text).toBe('hi')
    break
  }
  client.close()

app.socket() opens a thin client over the multiplexed socket WS. subscribe(name) yields the data frames for that socket, publish(name, msg) sends a client publish, and as(identity).socket() upgrades authenticated. Close the client (or stop() the app) to release the connection.

const res = await app.health()
  expect(res.status).toBe(200)
  expect(await res.json()).toMatchObject({ reachable: true })

app.health() hits GET /__abide/health, running your onHealth() hook against the real merged health document — a fast liveness assertion for your boot wiring.

  • origin — the http://localhost:<port> the app is listening on.
  • fetch(path, init?) — raw request against the live origin.
  • rpc.<name>(args?) — call a registered route with the correct verb; returns the decoded payload.
  • socket(name?) — a client over the multiplexed socket WS (subscribe / publish / ready / close).
  • health() — GET /__abide/health.
  • as(identity) — a sibling app that authenticates every request as identity (shares the same server + teardown, so onStop runs once).
  • stop() — shut the server down (runs onStop in discovery mode); always run it in an afterEach.

await createTestApp(config?) takes the explicit surfaces { routes, middleware, sockets, pages, layouts } — name only what a test needs — plus the discovery knobs { dir, lifecycle }. Omit every surface (or pass no argument) to load and boot the whole app.
src/ui/pages/rpc/mutations/page.abide:
Mutations

A mutation is POST, PUT, PATCH, or DELETE: args go in the JSON body and the handler runs on every call. If you have read Reads, you already know this page — a mutation is the same callable with the same surface, and the differences fit in one section at the end.

Define it, import it, call it. The four verbs are one shape differing only in HTTP method and intent — POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH partially updates, DELETE removes — so two are enough to show all four.

DELETE, keyed only by id. Args ride in the JSON body and the handler runs on every click — mutations retain nothing by default, which the last card on this page opts out of.

A mutation differs from a read in two things: the transport (method + body + a CSRF gate) and the default retention. A read retains forever; a mutation defaults to memo: {'{'} ttl: 0 {'}'} — coalesce identical concurrent calls, retain nothing — because running twice is what you usually want to avoid, not what you want cached.

So the difference is a default, not a capability. Set a ttl and a mutation retains like a read: here a repeat call hits the retained slot (the run number holds) while .refresh() re-runs the handler — read through .peek() / .refreshing(), the same probes a read uses.

The symmetry holds all the way out: a POST that yields jsonl is consumed by {'{'}#for await{'}'} exactly like a streaming read, with the same chunk probes. See Streaming.
src/ui/pages/rpc/page.abide:
Isomorphic RPC

rpc = memo + transport. An RPC is defined once on the server and called by the same name everywhere — in-process on the server, a fetch in the browser. The caching, coalescing, verbs, and probes are not RPC features: they are the memo underneath, and a bare memo() in the browser behaves identically. What an RPC adds is the wire, the schema, and the CSRF gate. Reads are cached and coalesced; mutations post their args and run every call. Live, interactive demos of the whole surface follow.

Each demo imports its RPC through the $server alias — e.g. import greet from "$server/rpc/greet" resolves to src/server/rpc/greet.ts. The same $server / $ui / $shared aliases work in any .abide or .ts file; see each demo's source tab.

  • Reads — GET/HEAD and the async-read forms in templates ({'{'}await fn(){'}'}, {'{'}fn.peek(){'}'}, {'{'}#await{'}'}) plus raw bypass and probes.
  • Mutations — POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE, and the full read/mutation symmetry when one opts into caching.
  • Responses — json, error, error.typed narrowing, redirect.
  • Streaming — jsonl/sse consumed with {'{'}#for await{'}'}, chunk probes, streaming mutations, and streaming SSR.
  • File uploads — a FormData mutation with file + text validation.
src/ui/pages/rpc/probes/page.abide:
Reactive probes

An RPC read is a memo with a transport, so it carries the same reactive read surface — the probes — as any memo. peek(args) is the non-blocking snapshot, pending(args)/refreshing(args) track first-load vs revalidation, error(args) holds a rejected read, and watch(args, cb) fires on every change. Same vocabulary as the generic-memo and socket probes — here over live GET fetches.

fn.peek(args) kicks the load and snapshots the value; fn.pending(args) and fn.error(args) report that same slot's live state as it resolves — all reactive, straight in the markup.

pending(args) is yes only while the first load is in flight; refreshing(args) is yes only while a re-fetch runs over a value that stays on screen. Load, then refresh — the value holds, refreshing flips to yes and pending stays no the whole time.

A read that fails returns a 400; the error probe holds it as an HttpError until invalidate clears the slot.

The real method fn.watch(args, cb) runs the callback whenever this slot's value changes (unlike watch(thunk), which auto-tracks an expression). Load, then refresh — the counter climbs and the watch callback fires.
src/ui/pages/rpc/reads/page.abide:
Reads

A read is GET or HEAD: args go in the URL, the result is cached and coalesced by the memo underneath. Define it once, call it by name on either side. This page is the call, then the four ways to render it, then the escape hatch.

Import the RPC and call it. On the server that is an in-process call; in the browser a fetch of the same name — and the read blocks SSR, so the value here is in this HTML before any JavaScript runs.

HEAD is the same read with no body — headers only, useful as a liveness ping. There is no HEAD helper: HTTP HEAD is GET minus the body, so the router derives it from the GET you already declared. The server tab here is an ordinary GET; the raw fetch beside it asks for HEAD and gets a status line with an empty body.

Waiting is the default and the one to write: {'{'}await fn(args){'}'} blocks the render, so the value lands in the server HTML — the string here is in this document before any JavaScript runs. Nothing suspends on the client; the text node fills when the read settles.

The await is not optional. Every expression slot is auto-awaited at runtime, so a bare {'{'}fn(args){'}'} renders the value too — but it types as Promise<T>, which dead-ends the moment you want a field. abide check rejects it, so there is one form, not two.

Not waiting is peek: a reactive T | undefined snapshot that never blocks. It returns whatever the slot holds and kicks a coalesced load — the value when the slot is warm (on the server too, if an earlier read of the same call settled during that render), undefined when it is cold. It is an ordinary value, so the placeholder is ordinary too: {'{'}fn.peek(args) ?? 'Loading…'{'}'}.

A read can also fail, and {'{'}#await{'}'} is where that becomes visible: three branches for the three states, so a pending message and an error path are structural rather than hand-rolled.

When you don't need a pending branch, the then binding folds into the opener. Same blocking behaviour as {'{'}await fn(){'}'}, but it binds the resolved value — the compact form for "I just want the value, typed".

Every form above goes through the memo — cached, coalesced, throwing on failure. fn.raw(args, init?) is the door out: the untouched Response, no caching and nothing thrown, so you read the status, headers and body yourself. See what the helpers put on the wire on Responses.

Beyond peek, a read carries the full reactive probe surface — pending, refreshing, error, watch — because it is a memo. They have their own page: RPC probes.
src/ui/pages/rpc/responses/page.abide:
Response helpers

A handler returns a plain value (auto-wrapped in json), makes that explicit with json, or ends the call another way entirely — error, error.typed and redirect all throw, and the router renders each at the status it asked for. Every one is consumed live in the browser below. Streaming responses (jsonl/sse) have their own page — see Streaming.

The default needs no helper at all: return a plain value and it is serialized as JSON. json(data, init?) is the same thing made explicit, for when you also want to set a status or headers.

A failure is a throw, not a return. error(status, message) does not hand a Response back — it throws an HttpError. That is what puts the failure in the memo slot's error channel and keeps it out of the value channel: an in-process caller reaches it with catch, fn.error() reports it, and a read at ttl: ∞ never retains a 422 as that slot's value forever.

Transport is the other half. The router renders the thrown error at its own status — before onError, because a declared 422 is not a bug in the app — and the browser proxy decodes the non-2xx back into the same HttpError, so the same catch reads the same status on both sides. Throwing also retires type machinery instead of adding it: a throw is never and a union absorbs it, so ({'{'} fail {'}'}) => fail ? error(503) : {'{'} greeting {'}'} still infers {'{'} greeting {'}'} with no brand and no conditional.

An untyped error tells you that it failed. error.typed(name, status, schema?) tells you which failure, by name — so a caller can narrow one kind from another with fn.isError(e, name) instead of matching on status codes or message strings.

The third kind of answer is "not here, there". redirect(url, status=302) throws a Redirect for the same reason error() throws an HttpError — a handler that redirects produced no value, so it must not resolve as one — and the router renders the 3xx. The browser fetch then follows it transparently — the resolved response reports redirected and the final url.

  • X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff and Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin — on everything
  • Cache-Control: private, no-cache + Vary: Cookie — the identity-scoped default, since a response may depend on who asked. Content-addressed /__abide/chunk/ assets opt out by declaring their own immutable long-cache
  • Strict-Transport-Security in production; X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN on HTML documents; a 405 carries Allow

Beyond each helper's own Content-Type / Location, the router stamps this baseline on every response at one choke point — and only where the response didn't already set it, so a handler, helper or middleware always keeps the last word.

Every card above shows the decoded result. fn.raw(args, init?) is the view underneath: the untouched Response, memo bypassed and nothing thrown, so you read the status line, headers and body yourself. Switch between the helpers and watch the status change — 200, 422, 429, 302 — each chosen by the helper, none by the framework.

The redirect button passes {'{'} redirect: "manual" {'}'} as init, the second argument of raw. The browser still won't show you the 302: the Fetch spec resolves a manual redirect to an opaque response with the status, Location and body withheld from JS. The wire carries all three — curl -i proves it — a reminder that raw hands you the browser's Response, not the server's.
src/ui/pages/rpc/streaming/page.abide:
Streaming

Any handler — read or mutation — can yield an AsyncIterable. Wrapped in jsonl or sse it becomes a replay-then-live stream: the browser callable decodes it back into an AsyncIterable consumed by {'{'}#for await{'}'}, identical on both sides. The same run is shared across concurrent and late viewers.

jsonl is see-through, so calling this read in the browser returns a replay-then-live AsyncIterable of the decoded chunks — iterated directly, with no fetch, reader or decoder to write. The button only delays the start so the chunks are visible arriving; .refresh() re-runs the source.

The same consumption over a different transport. An sse read is an AsyncIterable of the decoded data: frames — text/event-stream on the wire instead of application/jsonl, identical in the template.

The same sse endpoint is also consumable with the native EventSource DOM API — same frames on the wire, raw-DOM style.

A streaming read swaps the value probes for chunk probes — one per card: fn.peek(args) is the latest chunk, fn.chunks(args) is the transcript so far, and fn.done(args) reports whether the stream has closed.

The stream's current value: the most recent chunk, reactive, with no list to maintain. Reading it kicks the run; it advances as each tick lands.

Every chunk seen, as a snapshot array. Render it directly with a plain {'{'}#for{'}'} — same data as a {'{'}#for await{'}'}, snapshot rather than stream.

A status probe over the run: no while chunks are still arriving, yes once the stream finishes.

Streaming reaches mutations too: a POST that yields jsonl is consumed by {'{'}#for await{'}'} exactly like a streaming read, and .refresh() re-runs the job.

Streaming reaches the page render itself, too: a slow {'{'}#await{'}'} read that misses the SSR deadline flushes the shell then streams its resolved branch in — see Streaming SSR.
src/ui/pages/rpc/uploads/page.abide:
File uploads — multipart

A mutation whose single argument is a FormData accepts a file upload: the File rides in the multipart body, never in a JSON args object. The files schema validates the uploaded FILE (present, size, MIME); the JSON input schema validates the multipart TEXT fields (here caption is required and non-empty). Either failure is one 422 the client narrows to a ValidationError.

A native <form> builds the FormData for free: new FormData(form) harvests the avatar File and the caption text with no manual .set(). The browser then calls the SAME callable the server declares, which sends it as the raw multipart body — through the callable rather than the form's own action, because the CSRF gate wants a header a bare form submit can't forge.
src/ui/pages/sockets/page.abide:
Sockets

socket = channel + transport + per-room authorization. The pub/sub core, the rooms, and the reactive read surface are all the channel primitive; a socket adds the WebSocket mux, the clientPublish mediator, and the middleware that authorizes each subscribe and publish. The client imports the same socketsChat the server does: this demo subscribes by iterating it (for await (const m of socketsChat), over the WS mux), derives its status from the socket's reactive probes (pending() / refreshing() / error()), and publishes two ways: from the server (a POST RPC that calls socket.publish, arriving with via: "server") and from the client (the isomorphic socketsChat.publish(...), admitted by clientPublish — whose function form is the permission, mediating the untrusted message by stamping via: "client" and dropping empty text). Both feed one live log; "Clear local log" resets it.

One import, both sides: socketsChat is the same Socket<ChatMessage> the server holds, consumed here in the browser as an AsyncIterable, published to with .publish(), and probed with .pending() / .refreshing() / .error(). The status line is those probes — there is no connection bookkeeping to hand-roll.

The template block {'{'}#for await message of socketsChat{'}'} is the subscription — it rides the multiplexed WebSocket at /__abide/sockets transparently (one connection carries every named socket), appending each message as it arrives. No raw connection, no frames.

The socket keeps a tail of recent messages, so reloading this page replays them immediately — no re-publish needed.

Beyond iterating, a socket carries the reactive probe surface — peek() (latest message), chunks() (tail transcript), plus pending/refreshing/error. They have their own page: Socket probes.
src/ui/pages/sockets/probes/page.abide:
Reactive probes

A socket is a channel on the wire, and a channel implements the same reactive read surface a memo does — the probes — over a lossy hub instead of a keyed slot: peek() is the latest message, chunks() is the tail transcript, done() reports whether the topic is idle (no live subscription), and pending()/refreshing()/error() report connection status. Same vocabulary as the generic-memo and RPC probes. The peek/chunks demos share the one socketsChat topic, so a publish anywhere updates both.

The most recent message on the topic, reactive, with no list to maintain. Reading it opens the subscription, so it updates live as messages arrive.

The recent-message tail as a snapshot array (capped by the socket's tail). Render it directly with a plain {'{'}#for{'}'} instead of appending in a {'{'}#for await{'}'} — same data, snapshot rather than stream.

A status probe over the subscription lifecycle: yes while the topic is idle — no active read holds a subscription — and no once a live read opens one. It uses a standalone topic (untouched by the demos above) so it starts idle; open a subscription and it flips.
src/ui/pages/state/page.abide:
state — the owned value

The first of the three primitives. A state is a scope-free reactive atom that keeps only what it owns — derivation is memo's job, and pushing is channel's. It ships from abide/shared/state, so it is isomorphic: the same import in a page, a component, or a plain server .ts. Under each live demo is the exact source that powers it — read live from disk and highlighted on the server.

Declare it, write it, read it. Everything reading the cell updates — here, one text node.

Under the sugar a cell is callable: count() reads (and subscribes the enclosing memo/watch), count.set(next) writes, count.untracked() reads without subscribing. In a .abide <script> the compiler writes those calls, which is why these demos type the bare count; in a plain .ts you call the surface yourself — the server graph shows that form.

The optional second argument runs on every write, so the cell can never hold a value the transform wouldn't produce — clamping, rounding, normalising. One place for the invariant, rather than every call site.

Two component instances call state.shared("reactivity-tally", 0) with the SAME key, so they share one backing cell — bump either and both update. The value also syncs across other open tabs (via a BroadcastChannel); on the server .shared degrades to a per-render cell.

Reading a cell is how something subscribes to it. To push the other way — out of the graph, into a side effect — use watch.

A module-level state on the server is process-global — one value across every request. Right for a derived or immutable-source graph (see the server graph); for mutable per-request or per-user state reach for memo: {'{'} shared {'}'}, which is guarded and identity-safe.
src/ui/pages/templating/async/page.abide:
Async control flow

Three forms, split by how many values arrive and whether you need to see the waiting. {await} is the plain interpolation for one value — no branches, the server does the waiting. {#await} is for one value when you want a branch per promise state. {#for await} is for many — it appends each chunk of an async iterable as it lands. All three work identically during SSR and after hydration.

The common case needs no branches at all: await something during SSR and the value is in the initial HTML. Nothing suspends, nothing flashes — the server did the waiting.

In the browser a promise has states worth rendering, and the block gives you one branch each. Each click here reseeds a promise held in state: the pending branch shows, then the resolved or rejected one, and {:finally} renders once it settles either way.

Swap the promise for an async iterable and {#for await} appends each chunk as it arrives — no buffer to manage, no reader to drain. If the stream throws partway, {:catch} is appended after the chunks already emitted, so a failure never discards what arrived.

A stream has one question a promise doesn't: is it finished? done(stream) answers it reactively — false while a {#for await} is still draining that same stream object, true once it closes. Import it from abide/shared/done and call it in the template.

Streaming over a transport is the same two blocks with an RPC as the source — see Streaming, where {#for await} also picks up the SSR→client handoff and the chunk probes.
src/ui/pages/templating/bindings/page.ab:
Bindings & directives

Everything that connects a value to the DOM, in four steps: text out, attributes out, events in, and the two-way binds that do both. Each is wired to a live input, so it can be typed at, clicked, and checked.

{expr} — escaped text"} client="src/ui/demos/templating/bindings/EscapedTextDemo.abide">

The smallest binding there is: {'{'}expr{'}'} puts a value in a text node, escaped. It is reactive by construction — when the value changes, that one text node updates and nothing else is touched.

{html(...)} — raw HTML"} client="src/ui/demos/templating/bindings/RawHtmlDemo.abide">

Escaping is the default because it is the safe one. When you genuinely have markup, html(...) is the explicit opt-out — deliberately noisy at the call site, since that is where the trust decision lives.

name={expr} — reactive attribute"} client="src/ui/demos/templating/bindings/ReactiveAttrDemo.abide">

The same expression in an attribute position. One rule to remember: an attribute takes the whole value (name={'{'}expr{'}'}), and quoted values interpolate too, so class="btn {'{'}size{'}'}" mixes literal and reactive text.

class:name={cond} — toggle one class"} client="src/ui/demos/templating/bindings/ClassDirectiveDemo.abide">

Two directives narrow that to the cases you reach for constantly — toggling one class, setting one style property — so you don't rebuild a whole string to change one bit.

style:prop={value} — set one property"} client="src/ui/demos/templating/bindings/StyleDirectiveDemo.abide">

The same narrowing for one CSS property: style:prop={'{'}value{'}'} sets it directly, leaving the rest of the element's style alone.

{...expr} — spread attributes"} client="src/ui/demos/templating/bindings/SpreadAttrsDemo.abide">

And when the set of attributes is itself data, spread it. Useful for a component that forwards unknown attributes to its root element.

on<event>={fn} — native events"} client="src/ui/demos/templating/bindings/NativeEventsDemo.abide">

Values flow back on native DOM events. There is no synthetic event system and no custom names: onclick, oninput, and friends attach the real listener, and the event you receive is the real one.

bind:value={x} — the pair, in one directive"} client="src/ui/demos/templating/bindings/BindValueDemo.abide">

An attribute out plus an event in is such a common pair that it has its own form. bind:value is that pair for a text input: type, and the cell holds what you typed. Name the state var and you are done — the compiler synthesizes the write-back, so there is no accessor to hand-write for the ordinary case.

The same directive over the other input shapes. A checkbox binds a boolean; a radio group binds the one chosen value; a checkbox group binds an array of the checked ones — same name, shape follows the element.

A bind target resolves to one of four kinds, and both lanes read the one taxonomy: a node ref, a group, a boolean, or a value. checked and selected are the boolean pair — mirrored as a boolean attribute, present iff truthy, never stringified. They cannot be one target: an <input> keeps that state on .checked and an <option> on .selected, so the bind mirrors the property the target names.

The set is named rather than tested for, because a checked-only test is how selected came to mean two things at once: the server wrote a boolean attribute while the client fell through to the value bind, so the option rendered correctly and then had value="true" written over it on hydrate. A correct paint, clobbered by its own bind.

It is two-way in both directions, which took one more distinction: a bind reads the property off the element it is attached to, but listens on whichever element emits the event. For an <option> those are not the same node — selectedness changes because the user acted on the <select>, and events bubble up, so a listener on the option never sees it. Conflating the two makes the bind silently one-way: the mirror works, nothing throws, and the cell just never moves.

A radio group binds the ONE chosen value — same directive, and the shape follows the element.

Checkboxes sharing a name bind the ARRAY of what is checked. Nothing new to write; the element decided the shape.

bind:value={{get,set}} — a derived accessor"} client="src/ui/demos/templating/bindings/DerivedAccessorDemo.abide">

Finally, the escape hatch that makes the rest composable: a bind target does not have to be a cell. Give it {'{'} get, set {'}'} and you can validate, clamp, or reshape on the way through — the same accessor the compiler writes for you above, now yours to put logic in.

bind:element={cell} — the node itself"} client="src/ui/demos/templating/bindings/NodeRefDemo.abide">

When you need the DOM node — to focus it, measure it, or hand it to a library — bind:element gives it to you two ways. A cell receives the node; a function is called with it on mount and can return a teardown, which makes it the place to put per-instance setup.

bind:element={fn} — attach + teardown"} client="src/ui/demos/templating/bindings/AttachFnDemo.abide">

The function form is the per-instance hook: it is called with the node on mount and its return value is the teardown. Client-only by construction — it never runs during SSR — which makes it the place for DOM work a server render can't do.
Components

An inline component is a TitleCase {#component} taking a single props object — a reusable builder invoked as a tag <Name/>. It starts as "name some markup and use it twice" and ends as a first-class value you can pass around; every step below is that same declaration, asked to do a little more.

The whole idea: declare a builder, invoke it as a tag. TitleCase is what distinguishes it from an element — a lowercase name is a parse error, because lowercase is reserved for tags.

Props go in as attributes and stay reactive. Whatever sits between the tags fills the component's <slot/> — so a component can wrap content it knows nothing about. Both stay live after hydration.

One slot covers most cases; when you need two, you don't learn new syntax. A component written inside another's tags is passed to it as a same-named prop and invoked as a tag — named slots, falling out of the rule already in play. The leftover markup still fills the default <slot/>.

And when the props are already an object, spread them: {...obj} hands every key to the child, exactly as writing each name={value} by hand would. (On an element the same syntax sets attributes instead — see bindings.)

Nothing so far required a component to be a special kind of thing, and it isn't one. Pass it as a prop and let the receiver decide where to invoke it — the render-prop pattern, with no API behind it.

Because it is a value, a cell or memo can hold one. <Current/> where Current is a memo re-mounts whenever the derivation picks a different component — a dynamic component, again with no new syntax.

Since it is a value, it can also just be a field. A tag may be a member path — <row.Icon/> — so a row carries its own renderer as data instead of the list branching on a kind. The head is any binding in scope; TitleCase applies to the component's name, which is the last segment (<row.icon/> is a parse error).

And because it is an expression over bindings rather than an import, it is reactive for the same reason the memo-named tag above is: hand a row a different component and that one tag re-mounts. The by key hasn't changed, so the row's own <li> is never rebuilt — only the icon inside it. (A hyphen is what keeps a dotted tag an element: <my-el.foo> is legal HTML.)

A block body is ordinary markup, so nothing new applies: a {'{'}#for{'}'} invokes <Row/> once per keyed item, and a {'{'}#if{'}'} branch can declare its own component in the branch body. Keying still does what keying does — a reversed list moves each row's whole component range rather than rebuilding it, so a row that carries state keeps it.

An inline component owns the same two things a file component does, one level in: its <script> runs per invocation, so every tally has its own count, and its <style> reaches its own subtree — the .tally outside it keeps the class and none of the styling.
src/ui/pages/templating/conditionals/pag:
Conditionals

A conditional block picks exactly one branch and swaps the DOM when the state it reads crosses a threshold. Nothing is diffed by hand — the block reconciles fine-grained.

Error boundary — {#try}

A {#try} block renders its body; if any expression throws while the body mounts, the block switches to {:catch}. The {:finally} branch always renders. Here the body re-mounts on each click (keyed by the run id), so you can throw and recover on demand.

Each click bumps the run id, which is the keyed-list key, so the block re-mounts and re-evaluates from scratch. The run carries its own fail flag, so the body reads a fixed per-mount value rather than a shared mutable that could throw into an already-mounted block.

Lists

A {#for} block renders one body per item. Key it by identity to move DOM nodes on add / remove / reorder, or leave it keyless to map by position.

Keyed by item.id, the block reconciles by identity: adding, removing, and reordering move the matching DOM nodes instead of re-creating them.

Without a by clause the block maps by position — perfect for a plain value list.
src/ui/pages/templating/scripts/page.abi:
Branch-local <script>

A <script> at the top of a block body is that branch's setup: its state is created when the branch mounts and disposed when it goes, and inside a {#for} that means per iteration. It reuses the component's imports and reads its bindings, but nothing outside the branch can see what it declares — including a sibling branch that happens to use the same name.

Each row here owns a counter the component's own script has no name for. Adding a row adds a fresh one; the rows never share.

  • inside an element (<div><script>) — the element has no lifetime of its own; move it to the enclosing block.
  • after other markup in the body — it is setup, so it goes first.
  • a second one in the same body, or a second root-level <script> — merge them.
  • <script module> — it runs once per module, so it belongs at the top level.

A branch-local <script> must be the first node of a block body — the body of an {#if} branch, a {#for}, an {#await} branch, a {:case}, a {#try} branch, or a {#component}. That is the only position with a lifetime and a scope of its own, so anywhere else is a compile error rather than a script that quietly never runs.

It carries no import of its own — an import is module-level wherever it is written, so one here could only look conditional without being it. The component's imports are already in scope, which is why the demo above calls state without importing it a second time.

An assignment may span lines

Writing to a cell compiles to cell.set(…), so the compiler has to find where the right-hand side actually ENDS. A line break next to a continuation operator is not the end — a ternary broken before its ? and :, an operator with the break after it, a member chain broken before the ., an instanceof, an in, an as cast, or a template literal spanning lines are all one expression, exactly as they are in plain JavaScript.

This one is here because getting it wrong is silent. Severing the right-hand side at the break emits size.set( count > 2) followed by an orphaned ? "many" : "few" — which is not a syntax error, so nothing downstream complains. The cell is quietly set to the CONDITION and the branches evaluate against a discarded result. Every value on the page is still a value; it is just the wrong one, which is why the guard is a rendered demo rather than a compile check.
src/ui/pages/templating/styling/page.abi:
Scoped <style>

A component-scoped <style> is rewritten at build time: each selector gains a per-component attribute (.swatch → .swatch[data-ab-*]) and abide stamps that attribute on every element the component renders. The styles apply to this component only — on the server-rendered HTML and after hydration, never leaking to the rest of the page. (Tailwind classes still work alongside it.)

Two components render the same .swatch class; only the one that declared the rule is styled by it. The attribute doing that is stamped during SSR, so the scoping is already correct in the initial HTML — hydration changes nothing.

A <style> written inside a block scopes that subtree. An element carries every scope in force, so the component's own rule reaches into the branch and the branch's rule reaches nothing outside it — one direction, by construction.
src/ui/pages/watch/page.abide:
watch — the effect

The three primitives hold values; watch is how a value reaches something outside the graph. It is not a fourth primitive — it is the one escape hatch, and everything reactive in a rendered template is built on it. Like state, memo, and channel it ships from abide/shared/*, so it is isomorphic: a watch in a plain server module fires on the server, with no client involved.

Pass one function. It runs immediately and again whenever anything it read changes — nothing declares the dependency, the read is the declaration. The effect writes a cell it never reads, which is what keeps values flowing one way: in through the reads, out through the effect.

Pass a source thunk and two things change: the handler runs on change only — not on the initial read — and the dependency set is exactly what the thunk reads, whatever the handler touches.

The source is always a thunk (ADR 0025), mirroring memo(source, transform): same signature slot, same rule, second argument untracked in both.

Same inferred-or-declared split as memo; the two differ only in intent — a memo produces a value to be pulled, a watch performs an effect. That is why there is no separate "effect" primitive.

Several inputs are just what the thunk returns, exactly as in memo. Every read inside it is tracked, and the next/previous the handler already receives carry it — so a handler reads what changed by name, never by position.

An effect that takes something — a timer, a listener, a subscription — has to give it back. Either form may return a function, and that teardown runs at the two moments the resource must go: before every re-run, and when the effect is disposed. A component owns the effects its <script> creates, so disposal is that component going away — unmount in the browser, end of the request during SSR.

Changing the interval re-runs the effect, and the log shows stop landing before the next start. Unmounting the ticker fires it one last time. The same already happened on the server: this page's SSR ran the effect and cleared its interval when the request finished.

Holding one directly works the same way — watch returns a disposer, and calling it runs the teardown and detaches every read.

This is why the grammar has no onMount/onDestroy: the <script> body is setup and the returned teardown is cleanup, so the pair stays in one place. It is also why this demo holds a real timer with no is-this-the-browser branch. bind:element={'{'}fn{'}'} takes the same shape for a node.
